newsitem.title: CHINA: Gore says demands greater access to China market.
newsitem.headline: Gore says demands greater access to China market.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore said on Wednesday he had pulled no punches in talks on trade with Chinese leaders, telling Beijing it needed to do more to open its markets to American goods.
Gore told a news briefing his meetings with Chinese leaders included talks on the thorny issues of Beijing's growing trade surplus with the U.S. and its entry into the World Trade Organisation.
"I expressed the need of greater access to China's market for American goods and services," he said of his talks with Chinese President Jiang Zemin on Wednesday and Premier Li Peng on Tuesday.
Gore quoted U.S. trade figures, saying China's trade surplus with the United States was $39.5 billion last year.
He said Beijing's imports of American goods were not rising as fast as its purchases of products of other nations.
Beijing says its surplus with the U.S. was around $10 billion in 1996. Its figures exclude shipments through Hong Kong.
"I made the point that regardless of whatever differences might exist in the way we measure the deficit, there's no disagreement that it's large and it is growing," Gore said.
"That is why I did not pull any punches in my conversations on these issues with the Chinese," he said, adding that Beijing had promised better treatment for U.S. firms.

"Both President Jiang and Premier Li Peng made it clear in their comments that they intend to take further steps to open the Chinese market more to U.S. goods and services," Gore said without elaborating on what those steps would involve.
Chinese officials have said they were concerned the widening trade gap could spell trouble for Sino-U.S. relations.
On Tuesday, China ordered $685 million worth of Boeing jets and it signed a $1.57 billion joint venture agreement with General Motors to produce cars for the domestic market.
The vice president said both of these deals were helpful steps towards narrowing the trade gap.
Gore said Beijing's removal of trade barriers could help push through renewal of its preferential Most Favoured Nation (MFN) status that grants lower import tariffs to Washington's trading partners.
Gore said he did not think China's MFN status, which must be reviewed annually, was in peril this year.
"A lot will depend in the future on Chinese actions to open up the markets here on fair terms and to pay attention to the rising deficit with the United States," Gore said.

Gore said he was hopeful progress would be made in talks on Beijing's plans to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO) but added China had to make more concessions to win its much-coveted place in the trade body.
"We are committed to supporting Chinese membership in the World Trade Organisation on commercially meaningful terms," Gore said.
Beijing has sought to enter the WTO on more favourable terms accorded developing countries but many nations, including the United States, have said its economy is too big for such treatment.
